paragraphs: Nothing in the universe moves faster than light. And yet there are places that not even light can escape from. We call them black holes. In the next five minutes you will find out what they are, where they come from and how anyone can discover something that is, by definition, invisible. You will also learn why you really don’t need to worry about being swallowed by one.

sections.heading: What a black hole is
paragraphs: A black hole is a place in space where a huge amount of mass is squeezed into a very small space. This makes its gravity incredibly strong. To escape it, you would have to move faster than light. That is impossible, so everything stays inside.

That sounds abstract, so here is a comparison. If you throw a ball into the air, it falls back down. Only above a certain speed would it leave the Earth altogether. That speed is called the escape velocity. For the Earth it is a little over eleven kilometres per second. For a black hole it is higher than the speed of light.

The boundary beyond which there is no way back is called the event horizon. It is not a solid surface but an invisible line. How big it is depends only on the mass. The whole Earth as a black hole would be just about the size of a pea.

From a great distance, a black hole is actually harmless. It does not suck in everything around it. If you replaced the Sun with a black hole of the same mass, the Earth would simply keep orbiting it. It only becomes dangerous up close: there you would be stretched out like a noodle.

Around many black holes, it is anything but dark. Gas spiralling inwards forms a flat, fast-spinning disc. It rubs against itself and heats up to millions of degrees. This disc shines so brightly that it can be seen across vast distances. Some black holes also fire matter into space in narrow jets at nearly the speed of light. So the darkest objects in the universe are among the brightest sources of light we know.
What happens deep inside, nobody knows for sure. The theory predicts a point of infinite density. Many experts, however, see this as a sign that our physics reaches its limits there.
For science, that is a stroke of luck. No other object in space puts our theories of space and time to such a tough test.

sections.heading: How they form
paragraphs: Most known black holes are the remains of large stars. A star keeps itself in balance: gravity pushes inwards, while the energy produced inside it pushes outwards. Once the fuel is used up, gravity wins.

In stars with roughly twenty times the mass of the Sun or more, the core then collapses in a fraction of a second. The outer layers explode as a supernova. What remains is a black hole with a few to a few dozen solar masses.

Our Sun will not share this fate. At the end of its life it will shed its outer layers and slowly cool down as a small, hot white dwarf. It is simply not heavy enough to become a black hole. Stars like the Sun are far more common than giant stars, which is one reason black holes are relatively rare.

Our Milky Way alone could contain up to 100 million of these stellar-mass black holes. So far only around fifty have been found, almost all of them because they are paired with a star. Once formed, they can keep growing: they take in gas, swallow stars or merge with other black holes.

Then there are the giants. Supermassive black holes sit at the centres of galaxies and have millions to billions of solar masses. The black hole at the heart of our Milky Way is called Sagittarius A star. It has around four million solar masses and lies about 27,000 light-years from us. How such giants grew so large is one of the big open questions in astronomy. Some already existed when the universe was still young.

sections.heading: How to find the invisible
paragraphs: Because no light comes out, researchers look at the surroundings instead. It is a bit like spotting an invisible dancer. You cannot see him, but you can see his partner spinning around him. From her movement you can even work out how heavy he is.

Gas falling into a black hole gets extremely hot and glows in X-rays. That is how the first widely accepted black hole was found in the 1970s. It is called Cygnus X-1 and lies in the constellation of the Swan. There, an invisible partner keeps tearing gas away from a large star.

At the centre of the Milky Way, research teams spent decades tracking stars racing around an invisible point. Their orbits reveal that around four million solar masses are packed into a tiny space. That work won the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics.

In September 2015, the LIGO detectors in the United States picked up gravitational waves for the first time. These are tiny ripples in space that Albert Einstein had already predicted. They came from two black holes of about 36 and 29 solar masses merging with each other.

And in 2019 came the first picture. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes all over the world so that they act like a single telescope the size of the Earth. The image shows a glowing ring around a dark shadow in the galaxy Messier 87. In 2022 it was followed by an image of the black hole in our own Milky Way.

What remains open above all is the interior. There, Einstein’s theory of relativity and quantum physics contradict each other. Stephen Hawking also showed that black holes should give off a faint glow and could evaporate over unimaginably long periods of time. So black holes remain one of the most exciting puzzles in physics, and researchers around the world are still working on them.

keyTakeaways: A black hole is so dense that nothing, not even light, can escape once it crosses the event horizon.
Smaller black holes form when huge stars die, while giant ones sit at the centres of galaxies.
We find them through hot gas, the orbits of stars, gravitational waves and, since 2019, actual images.

Over the next ten minutes you will learn what black holes are, how they form, whether they are dangerous and how we manage to find them at all. This is not just exotic physics, either. Black holes shape entire galaxies, including our own.

sections.heading: How a star becomes a black hole
paragraphs: Most of the black holes we know are the remains of large stars. A star lives in a constant balance. Its own gravity tries to crush it. At the same time, deep inside, it fuses hydrogen into helium and later into heavier elements. The energy released pushes outwards and keeps the star stable.

Sooner or later every star runs out of fuel. For small stars like our Sun, the ending is relatively calm. The star swells up, sheds its outer layers and leaves behind a small, hot core called a white dwarf. The Sun will never become a black hole. It is far too light for that.

In very massive stars, gravity wins in the end. When the core stops producing energy, it collapses in a fraction of a second. The outer layers are blasted into space in a gigantic explosion called a supernova. For a short time, a supernova can outshine an entire galaxy.

What is left of the core depends on its mass. If the star was only just above the limit, the result is a neutron star: a ball the size of a city, so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes. If the star had roughly twenty times the mass of the Sun or more, nothing can stop the collapse. Then a black hole is born.

These pulsars showed for the first time that such extremely compact stellar remains really exist. That made the idea of even denser objects much more believable.

Supernovae have a surprising upside too. Many of the heavy elements formed in stars and in these explosions are scattered into space when the star blows up. Once formed, a black hole can keep growing. It takes in gas from its surroundings, swallows stars or merges with other black holes. Over time, small black holes become bigger ones. That is one way heavier black holes can build up step by step over time.

Exactly how many stars end up as black holes depends on details that are still being researched. These include what the star is made of and how much mass it loses through stellar winds during its life. One thing is certain: it only affects a small fraction of all stars, because very massive stars are rare.

For astronomers, these stellar corpses are valuable. Wherever a black hole forms, there used to be a giant star. So anyone who counts black holes also learns something about how the biggest stars live and die.

sections.heading: Small, medium, gigantic: the different types
paragraphs: Astronomers usually sort black holes by their mass. The first group are stellar-mass black holes. They form from stars, as described in the previous section. Their mass ranges from a few to a few dozen times that of the Sun.

At the other end of the scale are the supermassive black holes. They have hundreds of thousands to billions of solar masses and sit at the centres of large galaxies. That is why its surroundings glow fairly faintly. For comparison, the black hole in the galaxy Messier 87 has around 6.5 billion solar masses, more than a thousand times as much as ours.

How these giants grew so large is one of the most exciting questions in astronomy. Some already existed when the universe was less than a billion years old. paragraphs: A black hole is not really a hole at all. If anything, it is the opposite of empty space: nowhere else in the universe is so much mass squeezed into so little room. That extreme density is what gives a black hole its extraordinary gravity.

Albert Einstein gave us a vivid picture of gravity. Imagine a stretched trampoline with a heavy bowling ball in the middle. The fabric sags, and smaller balls roll towards the dip. Mass curves space and time in a similar way. In this picture, a black hole is a dip so steep that nothing can roll back out, not even light.

A comparison shows just how compact these objects are. If you squeezed the entire mass of the Earth into a black hole, it would be about the size of a pea or a fingernail. Our Sun, turned into a black hole, would shrink to a ball just a few kilometres across. Today its diameter is about 1.4 million kilometres.

One important point: a black hole does not suck up everything around it like a vacuum cleaner. From far away, its gravity acts exactly like that of any other object with the same mass. It only becomes dangerous when you get very close.

Black does not mean invisible, by the way. A black hole itself gives off no light. But its surroundings can shine brightly, and its gravity gives it away through the movement of nearby stars and gas. More on that later.

It is also remarkable how simple a black hole is from the outside. Physicists think it is essentially described in full by just its mass and its spin. Whether it was once a star, a cloud of gas or an asteroid, you can no longer tell from the outside. Hardly any other object in space is so plain and so puzzling at the same time.

That makes black holes a stroke of luck for science. Nowhere else can Einstein’s theory be tested under such extreme conditions. And nowhere else do we run so clearly into the limits of what we know about space and time.

paragraphs: Every black hole is surrounded by an invisible boundary called the event horizon. It is not a solid surface you could land on. It simply marks the distance beyond which there is no way back. Whatever crosses it can never leave the black hole again.

The name fits well. A horizon limits what we can see. Events inside this boundary can never reach us on the outside. No beam of light and no signal can make the journey out. Just as you cannot see a ship once it has sailed beyond the horizon at sea, we cannot see anything that has passed beyond this one.

The rule of thumb is simple: for every solar mass you add roughly three kilometres of radius. A black hole with ten times the mass of the Sun therefore has a radius of about 30 kilometres. That would fit over a large city.

For the black hole at the centre of our Milky Way, the rule of thumb gives a radius of around 13 million kilometres. That is about a fifth of the distance between Mercury and the Sun. The black hole in the galaxy Messier 87 is so big that its event horizon is almost 40 billion kilometres across. Our entire planetary system would fit inside with room to spare. The rule never changes, though: double the mass, double the radius.

Just outside the event horizon, light is bent so strongly that it can even orbit the black hole. This creates a thin, bright ring around the dark region. Seen from outside, the shadow of a black hole therefore looks bigger than the horizon itself, roughly two and a half times as big.

What happens beyond the horizon, we do not know. Albert Einstein’s equations predict that the mass at the centre collapses into a point of infinite density. Experts call this a singularity. Most physicists, however, see it as a sign that our theories reach their limits there.

One last nice detail: the event horizon is not a wall that things smash into. For someone falling in, space at that spot would at first look perfectly ordinary. What makes it special is that from here on, every possible path leads inwards. There is simply no direction left that points out.

sections.heading: What happens up close
paragraphs: From a safe distance, a black hole is harmless. A neat thought experiment shows this. If you replaced the Sun with a black hole of the same mass, the planets would simply carry on in their orbits. It would just get dark and very cold. A much gentler version of the same effect causes the tides on Earth: the Moon pulls a little harder on the side of our planet that faces it.

Quasars are extremely bright centres of distant galaxies that give off more light than hundreds of billions of stars put together. Today we know that a giant is feeding at their heart, and the gas shines just before it disappears.

The sight of such a disc is strange, too. Because the black hole bends light, from the side you do not just see the front of the disc. The part behind the black hole also becomes visible, as an arc above and below it. Computer simulations by NASA show this distorted view very impressively.

For space travel and science fiction, this means a flight past a black hole would be no problem at a sufficient distance. Space probes could even use its gravity to pick up speed, just as they do with planets today.

An everyday thought experiment helps. Throw a ball into the air and it falls back down. Throw it faster and it climbs higher. Above a certain speed it would leave the Earth for good. That threshold is called the escape velocity. For the Earth it is a little over eleven kilometres per second.

The more mass an object packs into a small space, the higher its escape velocity. For a black hole, the escape velocity is greater than the speed of light. And since nothing can travel faster than light, nothing gets out. In other words, a black hole is not defined by what it is made of, but by how tightly its mass is packed.

Albert Einstein gave us a vivid picture of gravity. Imagine a stretched trampoline with a heavy bowling ball in the middle. The fabric sags, and smaller balls roll towards the dip. Mass curves space and time in a similar way. In this picture, a black hole is a dip so steep that nothing can roll back out, not even light.

A comparison shows just how compact these objects are. If you squeezed the entire mass of the Earth into a black hole, it would be about the size of a pea or a fingernail. Our Sun, turned into a black hole, would shrink to a ball just a few kilometres across. Today its diameter is about 1.4 million kilometres.

One important point: a black hole does not suck up everything around it like a vacuum cleaner. From far away, its gravity acts exactly like that of any other object with the same mass. It only becomes dangerous when you get very close.

Black does not mean invisible, by the way. A black hole itself gives off no light. But its surroundings can shine brightly, and its gravity gives it away through the movement of nearby stars and gas. More on that later.

It is also remarkable how simple a black hole is from the outside. Physicists think it is essentially described in full by just its mass and its spin. Whether it was once a star, a cloud of gas or an asteroid, you can no longer tell from the outside. Hardly any other object in space is so plain and so puzzling at the same time.

That makes black holes a stroke of luck for science. Nowhere else can Einstein’s theory be tested under such extreme conditions. And nowhere else do we run so clearly into the limits of what we know about space and time.

sections.heading: The event horizon: the point of no return
paragraphs: Every black hole is surrounded by an invisible boundary called the event horizon. It is not a solid surface you could land on. It simply marks the distance beyond which there is no way back. Whatever crosses it can never leave the black hole again.

The name fits well. A horizon limits what we can see. Events inside this boundary can never reach us on the outside. No beam of light and no signal can make the journey out. Just as you cannot see a ship once it has sailed beyond the horizon at sea, we cannot see anything that has passed beyond this one.

How big the event horizon is depends only on the mass. This size is called the Schwarzschild radius, named after the German astronomer Karl Schwarzschild. The rule of thumb is simple: for every solar mass you add roughly three kilometres of radius. A black hole with ten times the mass of the Sun therefore has a radius of about 30 kilometres. That would fit over a large city.

For the black hole at the centre of our Milky Way, the rule of thumb gives a radius of around 13 million kilometres. That is about a fifth of the distance between Mercury and the Sun. The black hole in the galaxy Messier 87 is so big that its event horizon is almost 40 billion kilometres across. Our entire planetary system would fit inside with room to spare. The rule never changes, though: double the mass, double the radius.

Just outside the event horizon, light is bent so strongly that it can even orbit the black hole. This creates a thin, bright ring around the dark region. Seen from outside, the shadow of a black hole therefore looks bigger than the horizon itself, roughly two and a half times as big.

Real black holes also almost always spin, and some spin very fast. That is because the stars they formed from were already rotating. A spinning black hole drags the space around it along a little, like a spoon stirring honey. Researchers have been able to measure this effect indirectly as well.

What happens beyond the horizon, we do not know. Albert Einstein’s equations predict that the mass at the centre collapses into a point of infinite density. Experts call this a singularity. Most physicists, however, see it as a sign that our theories reach their limits there.

One last nice detail: the event horizon is not a wall that things smash into. For someone falling in, space at that spot would at first look perfectly ordinary. What makes it special is that from here on, every possible path leads inwards. There is simply no direction left that points out.

sections.heading: How a star becomes a black hole
paragraphs: Most of the black holes we know are the remains of large stars. A star lives in a constant balance. Its own gravity tries to crush it. At the same time, deep inside, it fuses hydrogen into helium and later into heavier elements. The energy released pushes outwards and keeps the star stable.

Sooner or later every star runs out of fuel. For small stars like our Sun, the ending is relatively calm. The star swells up, sheds its outer layers and leaves behind a small, hot core called a white dwarf. The Sun will never become a black hole. It is far too light for that.

In very massive stars, gravity wins in the end. When the core stops producing energy, it collapses in a fraction of a second. The outer layers are blasted into space in a gigantic explosion called a supernova. For a short time, a supernova can outshine an entire galaxy.

What is left of the core depends on its mass. If the star was only just above the limit, the result is a neutron star: a ball the size of a city, so dense that a teaspoon of it would weigh billions of tonnes. If the star had roughly twenty times the mass of the Sun or more, nothing can stop the collapse. Then a black hole is born.

Neutron stars are, in a way, the little siblings of black holes. They were discovered in 1967, when the student Jocelyn Bell picked up regular radio pulses from space. These pulsars showed for the first time that such extremely compact stellar remains really exist. That made the idea of even denser objects much more believable.

Supernovae have a surprising upside too. Many of the heavy elements formed in stars and in these explosions are scattered into space when the star blows up. New stars, planets and eventually people formed from that material. So the death of a big star creates a black hole and the building blocks for something new at the same time.

Once formed, a black hole can keep growing. It takes in gas from its surroundings, swallows stars or merges with other black holes. Over time, small black holes become bigger ones. That is one way heavier black holes can build up step by step over time.

Exactly how many stars end up as black holes depends on details that are still being researched. These include what the star is made of and how much mass it loses through stellar winds during its life. One thing is certain: it only affects a small fraction of all stars, because very massive stars are rare.

For astronomers, these stellar corpses are valuable. Wherever a black hole forms, there used to be a giant star. So anyone who counts black holes also learns something about how the biggest stars live and die.

sections.heading: Small, medium, gigantic: the different types
paragraphs: Astronomers usually sort black holes by their mass. The first group are stellar-mass black holes. They form from stars, as described in the previous section. Their mass ranges from a few to a few dozen times that of the Sun.

Our Milky Way alone probably contains a great many of them. About fifty have been found or are strongly suspected so far, almost all of them because they are paired with an ordinary star. Estimates suggest, though, that our galaxy may contain as many as 100 million stellar-mass black holes. Most of them are alone and therefore practically invisible.

At the other end of the scale are the supermassive black holes. They have hundreds of thousands to billions of solar masses and sit at the centres of large galaxies. Almost every large galaxy seems to have one. Our Milky Way does too. It is called Sagittarius A star and has about four million solar masses.

For a supermassive object, the Milky Way’s black hole is surprisingly quiet. It lies about 27,000 light-years away in the constellation Sagittarius and currently swallows only a little gas. That is why its surroundings glow fairly faintly. For comparison, the black hole in the galaxy Messier 87 has around 6.5 billion solar masses, more than a thousand times as much as ours.

How these giants grew so large is one of the most exciting questions in astronomy. Some already existed when the universe was less than a billion years old. That is really too little time to grow slowly from a single star. Perhaps they got a head start from the collapse of huge gas clouds or unusually massive stars in the early universe.

In between, researchers suspect a third group: intermediate-mass black holes with roughly a hundred to a few hundred thousand solar masses. They are hard to find because they neither shine especially brightly nor leave clear traces. There are first candidates, but for most of them there is no final confirmation yet. Finally, there are the purely hypothetical primordial black holes, which might have formed shortly after the Big Bang without any star at all.

These primordial black holes could be tiny, some only the size of an atom but with the mass of a mountain. Whether they really exist is an open question. Some researchers even think they could make up part of the mysterious dark matter. That has not been shown, though.

Put together, the range is astonishing. The smallest known stellar-mass black holes have only a few solar masses, while the biggest giants reach billions. That is a span of more than nine orders of magnitude. And yet they all obey the same laws. That is what makes black holes so fascinating: a single principle explains objects from the size of a city to ones bigger than our solar system.

sections.heading: What happens up close
paragraphs: From a safe distance, a black hole is harmless. A neat thought experiment shows this. If you replaced the Sun with a black hole of the same mass, the planets would simply carry on in their orbits. It would just get dark and very cold. The Earth would feel the same pull as it does today, because at that distance gravity depends only on mass.

Up close, it is a completely different story. There, so-called tidal forces take over. Gravity pulls much harder on the part of an object that is closer to the black hole than on the part that is further away. Near a small black hole, that difference would be deadly for a human. You would be stretched out like a noodle. Astronomers really do call this spaghettification. A much gentler version of the same effect causes the tides on Earth: the Moon pulls a little harder on the side of our planet that faces it.

Here is the surprise: near large black holes, the tidal forces at the event horizon are weaker. In theory you could cross the horizon of a supermassive black hole without noticing anything at first. You still could not come back, though.

Time also behaves strangely nearby. According to Einstein’s theory of relativity, time passes more slowly in strong gravity. If you watched a clock falling towards a black hole from far away, it would seem to tick slower and slower. For the clock itself, everything would run normally.

This slowing of time explains an old nickname. Because a falling star seemed to freeze at the horizon when seen from outside, black holes used to be called frozen stars. In reality everything disappears behind the horizon. Only the light that reaches us gets fainter and redder until it fades away completely.

Many black holes are surrounded by a disc of gas that slowly spirals inwards. The gas rubs against itself and heats up to millions of degrees. It glows brightly, especially in X-rays. Some black holes also fire matter out into space in narrow jets at almost the speed of light. The jet of the galaxy Messier 87 is around 5,000 light-years long. Strange but true: the darkest objects in the universe are often surrounded by the brightest light.

Around supermassive black holes, such a disc can reach enormous sizes. As early as the 1960s, researchers suggested that these discs power quasars. Quasars are extremely bright centres of distant galaxies that give off more light than hundreds of billions of stars put together. Today we know that a giant is feeding at their heart, and the gas shines just before it disappears.

The sight of such a disc is strange, too. Because the black hole bends light, from the side you do not just see the front of the disc. The part behind the black hole also becomes visible, as an arc above and below it. Computer simulations by NASA show this distorted view very impressively.

For space travel and science fiction, this means a flight past a black hole would be no problem at a sufficient distance. Space probes could even use its gravity to pick up speed, just as they do with planets today.

sections.heading: How to find something invisible
paragraphs: If no light comes out of a black hole, how can you prove it is there at all? The answer is through its effect on its surroundings. Today there are four ways of doing that.

It is a bit like spotting an invisible dancer on a stage. You cannot see him, but you can see his partner spinning around him. From her movement you can even work out how heavy he is. Astronomers do exactly that, only with stars, gas and light instead of dancers.

The first way is through X-rays. When a black hole is paired with a star, it pulls gas off that star. The gas heats up and gives off X-rays before it vanishes. That is how the first widely accepted black hole was found in the 1970s: Cygnus X-1 in the constellation Cygnus, the Swan. The X-ray source itself had already been discovered in 1964 during a short rocket flight.

The second way is through the orbits of stars. Starting in the 1990s, two research teams led by Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez tracked stars at the centre of the Milky Way. To do so, they had to look through thick dust using large telescopes and special techniques. The stars there race along tight orbits around an invisible point. From those orbits, the teams worked out that around four million solar masses sit in a tiny space. Genzel and Ghez received the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for this work.

The third way is through gravitational waves, tiny ripples in space-time itself. In September 2015 the two LIGO detectors in the United States picked up such a signal for the first time. It came from two black holes with about 36 and 29 solar masses merging more than a billion light-years away. What remained was a black hole of around 62 solar masses. The missing three solar masses or so were radiated away as gravitational waves in a fraction of a second.

The fourth way is an actual picture. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio telescopes all over the world into a virtual telescope the size of the Earth. In April 2019 the team released the first image of a black hole: the shadow at the centre of the galaxy Messier 87. This black hole is about 55 million light-years away and has around 6.5 billion solar masses.

In May 2022 came the image of Sagittarius A star, the black hole in our own galaxy. It lies around 27,000 light-years from us. The image confirmed that its four million solar masses are packed into a region smaller than Mercury’s orbit around the Sun. Both images show a glowing ring of hot gas with a dark spot in the middle. That spot is the shadow the black hole casts on its own glow.

There is an enormous amount of work behind these images. The data came from observations made in 2017 with eight radio telescopes at six sites around the world. There was so much data that it had to be flown around on hard drives instead of being sent over the internet. For Sagittarius A star alone, about three and a half petabytes were collected. Over several years, teams used different methods to turn that into a picture.

sections.heading: A short history of a crazy idea
paragraphs: The idea is older than you might think. As early as 1783 the English clergyman and natural philosopher John Michell wondered whether there might be stars so heavy that their light could not escape. He called them dark stars. A little later the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace had similar thoughts. Both were still working with Isaac Newton’s theory of gravity. Their reasoning was simple: if light is made of tiny particles, a strong enough gravity should be able to hold them back.

The modern story begins with Albert Einstein. In 1915 he published his general theory of relativity. It describes gravity not as a force but as a curvature of space and time. Just a year later, Karl Schwarzschild found a solution to these equations that describes a black hole. He worked it out while serving as a soldier in the First World War.

Many people still regarded this solution as a mere mathematical curiosity. Einstein himself doubted that nature would actually produce such a thing. In 1939 Robert Oppenheimer and his colleagues showed that a heavy, burnt-out star really can collapse without limit. In the 1960s Roger Penrose proved mathematically that black holes are a robust prediction of relativity and not just a special case. He too received the Nobel Prize for this in 2020.

In the 1960s, new momentum came from observations. Astronomers discovered quasars, incredibly bright points in distant galaxies. In 1964 Yakov Zeldovich and, independently, Edwin Salpeter suggested that gas pouring into a giant black hole could supply this energy. Shortly afterwards, Zeldovich and Igor Novikov proposed searching for black holes in pairs of stars. The target was an invisible partner that shines brightly in X-rays.

Exactly such a system was soon found. By 1972 astronomers had collected enough data on Cygnus X-1. The mass of the invisible partner was too great for a neutron star. That made Cygnus X-1 the first serious candidate for a stellar-mass black hole. In the same year, Stephen Hawking proved that, under the classical laws, the area of an event horizon can never shrink. Black holes now had rules reminiscent of thermodynamics.

The catchy name was popularised by the American physicist John Wheeler in 1967. Before that, people often spoke of frozen or collapsed stars. With the new term and the first X-ray observations, black holes went from thought experiment to an established part of astronomy.

Since then the picture has become ever sharper. What started as a footnote to Einstein’s theory has become one of the central fields of astrophysics. Several recent Nobel Prizes are closely linked to black holes. And the story is far from over.

It is remarkable how often theory and observation have pushed each other forward. Sometimes the calculation came first and the proof decades later. Sometimes researchers stumbled on a signal they could not explain at first. With black holes, both have happened again and again.

sections.heading: What we still don’t know
paragraphs: Despite all these successes, black holes are full of open questions. One of the most famous comes from Stephen Hawking. In 1974 he showed that, because of quantum effects at the event horizon, black holes should in fact give off a very faint glow. This Hawking radiation means they slowly lose mass over unimaginably long periods and could eventually evaporate.

For black holes with the mass of a star, however, this would take far longer than the universe has existed so far. That is why Hawking radiation has never been measured. For large black holes it is far too weak.

The smaller a black hole, the hotter it would be according to Hawking, and the faster it would evaporate. Very small primordial black holes from the early universe might therefore be reaching the end of their lives right now. Hawking suggested they would then explode in a final burst of radiation. Space telescopes have searched for such signals but have not found a clear one yet.

The idea leads to a deep puzzle known as the information paradox. Quantum physics says that information can never be completely lost. But if a black hole evaporates entirely, everything that ever fell into it seems to be gone. How the two fit together is still unresolved. Researchers have proposed many possible solutions, but none has been confirmed.

Behind this lies an even bigger problem. Relativity describes the very large, quantum physics the very small. Inside a black hole the two meet, and there they contradict each other. A theory that unites both does not exist yet. That makes black holes something like natural laboratories for the physics of the future.

Observations are continuing too. The Event Horizon Telescope is due to get extra antennas so it can deliver sharper images and even movies. Gravitational-wave detectors now regularly pick up signals from merging black holes. Every new measurement is also a test of Einstein’s theory. So far it has passed every single one.

Another puzzle is the early giants. New telescopes keep finding supermassive black holes that existed very soon after the Big Bang. How they became so heavy so quickly is something we do not yet understand. Perhaps the young universe offered ways of forming them that no longer exist today.

New instruments are planned for the coming years. The European Space Agency is working on LISA, a gravitational-wave detector in space. It is mainly meant to track down merging supermassive black holes, whose signals oscillate too slowly for detectors on Earth. We might soon be able to hear galaxies merging together with their giants.

In the end, black holes show something fundamental about science. An idea that even its discoverers thought unrealistic has been confirmed step by step. First with mathematics, then with X-rays, with stellar orbits, with gravitational waves and finally with pictures. Who knows what surprise the next measurement will bring.

Perhaps that is the most beautiful thing about black holes. They hide their interior, and precisely because of that they force us to understand better how the universe works on the smallest and the largest scales. Perhaps one day they will help us answer some of the deepest questions about the universe itself.

keyTakeaways: A black hole is so dense that its gravity lets nothing escape from behind the event horizon, not even light.
Small black holes form from dying giant stars, while supermassive ones like Sagittarius A star sit at the centres of galaxies.
X-rays, stellar orbits, gravitational waves and real images prove they exist, yet their interior remains one of the biggest puzzles in physics.
